modalLead: Widgets answer to the right-click and the keyboard the way categories do, Health can be told to stop reporting a condition you have already decided about, and the server log finally says what it is doing in sentences you can act on.

items.text: Right-click a widget and it says what it can do. Rename it, switch it between one and two columns, fold it, open its settings, or close it — all from its own header, without going to Config → Widgets to find the switch. The name you give it is the name that appears there too.

The keyboard goes into a widget, not around it. Arrow keys step into a widget and move through its rows the way they move through a category, Enter opens the link under the cursor, and the same actions the right-click menu offers have keys of their own. Widgets used to be the one block the keyboard skipped.
A short tour explains what a custom widget can reach. It opens the first time you visit Config → Widgets and shows what a widget of your own can pull in from your own services.
The uptime widget fills itself in. It used to sit there asking you to open Health once before it would show anything. It now arrives with its figures already in place.
Switching a widget between one and two columns keeps your place. The page jumped to the top every time, so a widget halfway down took you away from what you were reading.

A bookmark can be told to stop reporting one condition. A link you know is fine but keeps being flagged as stale, unused or broken can be set aside with n or z, or from the row's menu. It stays in your collection and keeps being checked — it simply stops raising that one flag. An Ignored filter shows everything you have set aside, and one click puts a bookmark back.
Acting on a row leaves you at that row. Saving a copy or changing a setting sent you back to the top of the list, so finding your place again was part of every action.
The row menu is short enough to read. It had grown long enough to need scrolling on many screens, which meant the option you wanted was often out of sight.

Saving a copy says what happened. A copy that cannot be made now names the reason, pages up to 52 MB can be saved where the limit used to be 32 MB, and a page that saved as an empty shell says so instead of leaving you to discover it on opening.
Every saved copy can be cleared at once. Config → Bookmarks → Local copies has a button that removes them all, after asking and telling you how many and how much space it frees.

The server log says what it is doing. Every line now names how serious it is and which part of nextDash it came from — checked 110 bookmarks, 2 failed, or dash.example could not be saved — written for someone running nextDash rather than reading its source. Whole parts of the server that used to pass in silence now say what they did: a check round, a feed poll, an import, a saved copy, a scheduled backup, a failed write to disk.

You choose how much the server writes. Detail level under Server log offers Quiet, Normal and Verbose, and takes effect on the very next line — no restart, nothing to change in your setup. A line beneath it says what is being recorded as of now, so “why do I see nothing” has one answer instead of two guesses.

The activity trail is picked from a list. Twelve things can be recorded — changes, check results, health rounds, imports, feed polls, saved copies, backups, failed writes, and more — each with its own switch. Changes and check results are on to begin with, and Reset panel puts the list back whenever you have wandered from it.
Coming back to the window leaves you where you were. Switching to another window and back sent the dashboard to the top, which was disorienting halfway down a long page.
A failed load says why, and only when you asked for one. Failed to load bookmarks for this page had been appearing on its own while nothing was actually wrong.
